raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old man was attended in the dental clinic complaining of symptomatic oral lesions with two months in duration. The intraoral physical examination revealed diffuse, friable, vegetative areas on the right upper alveolar ridge, hard palate, and left inferior alveolar ridge (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)). His medical history revealed a diagnosis of tuberculosis about a month ago in which the expectorated sputum smears were positive for bacteria and acid-fast bacilli. In addition, at the time of diagnosis of tuberculosis, the patient had a significant weight loss and asthenia. The patient was under antibacterial therapy (oral isoniazid (INH) 225 mg/day, rifampicin (RFP) 450 mg/day, pyrazinamide 1,200 mg/day, and ethambutol (EB) 825 mg/day). Testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection was negative. Furthermore, the patient confirmed smoking and chronic alcoholism. He worked as a night flow controller on the side of a highway and lived very close to the countryside. After knowing the patient's medical history, the main hypothesis for oral lesions was tuberculosis.
An incisional biopsy of the right upper alveolar ridge showed connective tissue with intense inflammatory infiltrate with a granulomatous pattern, consisting of giant multinucleated inflammatory cells and vacuolated macrophages, with innumerable fungi suggestive of H. capsulatum (Figures 2(a) and 2(b)). Staining slides with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) (Figures 2(c) and 2(d)) and Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver were positive for the morphological characteristics of H. capsulatum. In addition, the immunohistochemical reactivity to Histoplasma using polyclonal antibody was positive; for polyclonal P. brasiliensis, Leishmania spp. and Calmette-Guerin bacillus were negative. The diagnosis of oral histoplasmosis was established. We did not search for fungi in other biological samples.
Initially, the drug was maintained for tuberculosis and prescribed fluconazol (400 mg/day) for seven months for treatment of oral histoplasmosis. During the follow-up, when a gradual increase in body weight was noted, fluconazole was substituted for itraconazole 200 mg/day for eight months with the resolution of oral histoplasmosis lesions. The clinical control one year after initiation of itraconazole treatment can be seen in Figures 3(a) and 3(b). One year after the initial treatment of tuberculosis, the patient was cured.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old man presented to a dental clinic with a 2-month history of symptomatic oral mucosal lesions, asthenia, and significant weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed painful oral lesions 2 months prior to presentation, along with significant weight loss and asthenia. One month prior to dental evaluation, he was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis via AFB-positive sputum smears and started on 4-drug anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol).
subjective.past_medical_history: Pulmonary tuberculosis diagnosed 1 month prior. Social/occupational history: Smoker and chronic alcohol user; worked as a nighttime highway traffic flow controller and lived near the countryside.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for painful oral lesions, significant weight loss, and asthenia. Home medications: oral isoniazid 225 mg/day, rifampicin 450 mg/day, pyrazinamide 1,200 mg/day, and ethambutol 825 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: Intraoral exam: diffuse, friable, vegetative lesions involving the right upper alveolar ridge, hard palate, and left inferior alveolar ridge.
objective.routine_investigations: HIV serology: negative; prior expectorated sputum smears positive for bacteria and acid-fast bacilli.
objective.advanced_workup: Incisional biopsy of the right upper alveolar ridge (H&E, PAS, GMS, and IHC): connective tissue with intense granulomatous inflammatory infiltrate containing multinucleated giant cells and vacuolated macrophages filled with innumerable yeast organisms positive on PAS, Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver, and polyclonal anti-Histoplasma immunohistochemistry (negative IHC for Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, Leishmania spp., and BCG).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Oral histoplasmosis coexisting with active pulmonary tuberculosis in an HIV-negative patient. Confirmation: Right upper alveolar ridge biopsy demonstrating intracellular yeast forms on H&E, PAS, and GMS stains with positive polyclonal anti-Histoplasma immunoreactivity. Plan & clinical course: Continued 4-drug anti-tuberculosis therapy while treating oral histoplasmosis initially with oral fluconazole 400 mg/day for 7 months, followed by substitution with oral itraconazole 200 mg/day for 8 months, achieving complete resolution of the oral lesions and cure of tuberculosis at 1-year follow-up.
